newsitem.title: CHINA: China raises defence budget by 14.7 percent.
newsitem.headline: China raises defence budget by 14.7 percent.

text.p: China will increase its defence budget in 1997 by 14.7 percent and has called on regional officials to do their utmost to support the army, Chinese sources said on Friday.

In a budget speech just days after the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, Finance Minister Liu Zhongli will say on Sunday that Beijing will spend 80.57 billion yuan ($9.7 billion) on defence this year, an increase of 14.7 percent on last year's budget, the sources said.

The 1997 budgeted figure was 12.7 percent higher than actual spending in 1996, Liu will say. A part of his prepared budget speech to parliament, the National People's Congress, was seen in advance by Reuters.
The increase comes as President Jiang Zemin, Deng's successor, is trying to strengthen his position and to win the support of the military.

China raised its defence budget by 11.3 percent in 1996, compared with increases of 14.59 percent in 1995 and 22 percent in 1994. Actual defence spending in 1996 was 71.503 billion yuan ($8.6 billion), which exceeded the budget by 2.4 percent, Liu is to say.

Beijing defends it large annual percentage increases in military spending by saying the base figure is still low and inflation cuts purchasing power. Retail inflation in 1995 was 14.8 percent but was reined in to 6.1 percent last year.
China vehemently denies charges that it is becoming a threat in Asia or to the rest of the world, but its military build-up has caused anxiety among neighbours.

The three million-strong People's Liberation Army , the biggest in the world, ruffled feathers in the region in March 1996 when it held missile tests and war games close to Taiwan just before the island's presidential election.
In his annual government work report to be presented more than 2,900 deputies in parliament on Saturday, Premier Li Peng will stress the importance of the military.

"Various levels of government must support and coordinate with the People's Liberation Army... to further strengthen defence capability," Li will say, according to parts of his speech seen in advance.
"We must attach importance to construction of frontier and coastal defence to protect the territorial integrity of the country."

Politburo standing committee member Liu Huaqing, a vice-chairman of the powerful Central Military Commission, emphasised on Friday the importance of modernising and developing a high-technology military.

"We must work even harder to grasp (high technologies) in order to improve the overall quality of the army and enhance the level of its modernisation," the official Xinhua news agency quoted Liu as saying.
Quoting Deng , whose power base lay with the military, Liu declared that "stability took precedence over everything else."
